title: The Matthew Effect (Cumulative Advantage)
description: “The rich get richer and the poor get poorer.” Small initial advantages compound over time, creating widening gaps in status, resources, and recognition—often beyond what is deserved by merit alone.
shortDescription: “The rich get richer and the poor get poorer.” Small initial advantages compound over time, creating widening gaps in status, resources, and recognition—often beyond what is deserved by merit alone.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: “The rich get richer and the poor get poorer.” Small initial advantages compound over time, creating widening gaps in status, resources, and recognition—often beyond what is deserved by merit alone.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A scientist gets early recognition for a decent paper. Suddenly, they get more grant money, better collaborators, and more citations—not because their work is dramatically better, but because visibility feeds itself.
An employee gets a lucky early project with high visibility. Then they’re first in line for promotions. A colleague who started slightly later never catches up.
In social media, an account with a few early followers gets more algorithmic push, snowballing into a huge following while equally good accounts stay small.

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: The already‑recognized get asked to speak, write, and lead—giving them even more recognition.
Small initial differences in performance become large differences in reputation.
Those without early advantages struggle to break in, regardless of talent.

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “They’re a known quantity.” (meaning: we trust them because others trust them)
“You need experience to get the job, but you need the job to get experience.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You’re working equally hard but getting nowhere near the rewards of someone who started slightly ahead.
Reputation seems to feed on itself, independent of recent performance.
You’re judging someone’s ability by their credentials rather than their output.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Sociologist Robert Merton named it after the Gospel of Matthew. Small advantages lead to more opportunities, which lead to more advantages. It’s a positive feedback loop that amplifies inequality over time.

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: If you’re behind, focus on getting one small, visible win that can act as a seed.
If you’re ahead, recognize that your position isn’t pure merit—and give opportunities to those who haven’t had the early break.
In hiring or promotion, evaluate people’s raw work, not just their reputation or network.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming that those at the top are inherently superior; they may have just caught an early wave.
Giving up because you haven’t had a break. The effect makes it harder, not impossible.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: Two journalists start at the same time. One gets assigned to cover a major story by chance; the other gets routine assignments. A year later, the first has a Pulitzer nomination and a book deal. The second is still covering local news. The difference in current status is enormous, but the initial seed was luck.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: Success snowballs, and the snowflake that starts the avalanche is often a gust of wind, not a mountain of merit. Recognize the wind, and you can learn to catch it.
